column1: Optimal Inflation Target: Insights from an Agent‑Based Model

The thesis titled Optimal Inflation Target: Insights from an Agent-Based Model by Jean-Philippe Bouchaud  Stanislao Gualdi  Marco Tarzia  and Francesco Zamponi explores the appropriate level of inflation that central banks should aim for  using a simplified Agent-Based Model (ABM) of the economy. The study examines how different parameters  particularly inflation expectations  influence macroeconomic behavior. Without active monetary policy  the model can exhibit various states  such as high inflation/high output or low inflation/low output  and can also show hyper-inflation  deflation  and business cycles between these states. The introduction of a central bank with a Taylor rule-based inflation target is then analyzed to observe its effects on aggregate variables.

The main finding is that setting inflation targets too low can be harmful to an economy monitored by a central bank  as evidenced by persistent under-realization of inflation  which may resemble current macroeconomic conditions. Higher inflation targets are shown to improve unemployment rates and reduce episodes of negative interest rates. The results are compared with predictions from the standard Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium (DSGE) model.

The thesis is structured as follows: an introduction discusses the common practice of central banks targeting a 2% annual inflation rate and the lack of clarity on why this specific target is chosen. The introduction also highlights the debate on whether higher inflation targets could have provided more room for monetary policy during crises. The paper then delves into methodological remarks and the scope of the study  followed by a recap of the Mark-0 model  which is the basis for the ABM used in the study.

The model includes components such as central bank policy  household behavior  firm behavior  financial fragility  production updates  price updates  and wage updates. The parameters of the model are detailed  and the native state of the economy is described. The study then explores inflation targeting  examining both high inflation/high output and low inflation/low output native states  and provides an economic interpretation of these states. The discussion includes Phillips Curves and a comparison with DSGE models  concluding with the assertion that higher inflation targets generally lead to better economic outcomes.

The thesis acknowledges the complexity of defining optimal inflation and the importance of the modeling framework used to describe the economy. It critiques the standard DSGE models for their assumptions and highlights the advantages of ABMs  which can capture interaction-induced collective effects and endogenous crises. The study emphasizes the need for academic research to inform policy decisions on optimal inflation levels  as highlighted by statements from policymakers like Federal Reserve Chairwoman Janet Yellen.

In conclusion  the thesis argues for a reevaluation of inflation targets  suggesting that higher targets could be beneficial in reducing unemployment and avoiding negative interest rates  while also acknowledging the challenges and uncertainties involved in such policy decisions. The study contributes to the ongoing debate on inflation targeting by providing insights from an agent-based modeling perspective.
